I am 57 years old, and I have worked these 5 mu in Quzhou County for 35 years. My wife and I do most of the farm work; my son works in a factory in Handan and sends money home, so we are not desperate, but this land still feeds us and must pay for itself. We have a well, and I pump water when I must, but electricity is expensive, so I do not waste water on crops that do not need it.

It is early October. The maize is harvested and dried, so next week I will run the rotary tiller over the whole 5 mu to prepare the seedbed for winter wheat. I will sow an improved variety — I have used Shimai 22 for several years and it does well here — at about 25 jin per mu. I spread compound fertilizer as a base, around 50 kg per mu, and at green-up or jointing in the spring I topdress with urea or ammonium bicarbonate. That gives the wheat enough nitrogen, about 18 kg per mu, plus 6 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium. The soil here is decent but always needs nitrogen. I irrigate three times: once before winter if the autumn is dry, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I spray herbicide after sowing, and if I see aphids or powdery mildew in the spring, I spray once more.

After wheat harvest in early June, there is no time to rest. I sow hybrid maize — Denghai 605 or something similar — immediately with the no-till seeder, using one package of seed per mu. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing, about 80 kg per mu, and sometimes I add a little urea at the big trumpet stage if the leaves look yellow. Total nitrogen is about 20 kg per mu, phosphorus about 5 kg, potassium about 4 kg. Maize needs less care than wheat. I irrigate twice, at jointing and at tasseling; the summer rains help, but you cannot rely on them. One herbicide spray and one insecticide spray is enough if you watch the fields.

I expect about 1,000 kg of wheat per mu and 1,100 kg of maize per mu in a normal year. That is what I have been getting. It is not the highest in the village, but it is steady, and I do not throw money at inputs I do not need.
